children: By Mariah Timms, Philip Wegmann and Sadie Gurman

President Trump called for Democratic former Rep. Mary Peltola to be criminally prosecuted and removed from the ballot in the Alaska Senate race, ramping up his allegations of election interference days before the midterms.

The president made his comments hours after the New York Times reported that Peltola campaign staffers were part of an effort to try to recruit an independent challenger with the same name as Republican Sen. Dan S. Sullivan, a move that critics allege was intended to confuse voters.
A candidate on the ballot for the midterm elections, Dan J. Sullivan Jr., has the same first and last name as the Republican incumbent.

"I think they should be prosecuted. To me, that's voter fraud at the highest level," Trump told reporters on Wednesday, referring to Peltola and Dan J. Sullivan Jr. Trump also said both "should be taken off the ballot."
In a statement following the Times report, Peltola's campaign said it has had "no involvement with either Sullivan campaign." The Justice Department declined to comment.

During an interview with Fox News earlier Wednesday, Attorney General Todd Blanche accused Democrats of election interference. "They are cheating. Let's just call it what it is. They are trying to take votes away from the incumbent, not by running an election and not by running on issues, but by putting up a person with the same name so that they confuse Alaskans," Blanche said.

Trump said last week that he had directed the Justice Department to file a lawsuit over the Alaska ballot. The lawsuit, which cites claims of potential voter confusion over the two Sullivans, has asked the court to delay certifying the election result if the incumbent Republican senator seems likely to lose — and the number of votes cast for the other Sullivan might change the outcome. Alaska uses a ranked-choice system, in which voters rank candidates in order of preference.
The Justice Department said in court filings Wednesday afternoon it plans to seek information from the Peltola campaign on the allegations in the New York Times report as part of the lawsuit.

The Alaska Republican Party had previously tried to get Dan J. Sullivan Jr. off the ballot, arguing he was a Democratic plant. He denied that in an interview with The Wall Street Journal last month. The Alaska Supreme Court ruled both Sullivans could appear on the ballot. Both candidates are listed with middle initials, and the current senator's party affiliation and incumbent status appear next to his name.

The Justice Department in August issued grand jury subpoenas as part of an investigation into whether Dan J. Sullivan Jr. entered the race to confuse voters and steal votes from Sen. Dan S. Sullivan, an official familiar with the matter said.
The Alaska Senate race is one of the most closely watched contests in the country, with polls showing a tight race as Democrats try to wrest back control of the chamber from Republicans.

Alaska's other senator, Republican Lisa Murkowski, slammed the Peltola campaign after the New York Times report. "Alaskans deserve the honest truth from Mary and her campaign — what has been revealed is a pattern of lies and coverups and a culture of deception that belongs nowhere in our elections or among our elected officials," she said in a statement.
